name: Gamāle Khām
confidence_why: Wilde 2011 says outright that Gamāle Khām stress is "yet to be determined with any certainty", Wilde 2016 and Wilde 2017 describe phonation and report the language as atonal without ever locating word stress, and Watters 1973 treats Takāle Khām clause syntax and never mentions Gamāle, so no published description says where, or whether, this language stresses words.

catalog_quote: [Wilde 2016 §2.3, p.135] Gamāle Khām contrasts between modal (14a) and breathy (14b) phonation. ... In Wilde (2011: 279,287) I considered whether Gamāle Khām phonology may also feature tense phonation. However, further investigation has led to the conclusion that this is not the case, and that the stiff voice or laryngealisation is an idiolectal tendency and/or caused variably by syllable-final glottal restriction. Unlike Takāle Khām as described by Watters (1971; 1985; 2002), Gamāle Khām is an atonal language. A pitch distinction was encountered with any certainty only once in the corpus (15a–b). ... [Wilde 2017 §2.1.3, p.71] Vowel length is non-contrastive. For the most part also pitch is non-contrastive. A pitch distinction was encountered with any certainty only once in the corpus (19a–b). ... audit.reasoning: The record codes Gamale Kham not determinable because none of the three dedicated phonological descriptions (Wilde 2011, 2016, 2017) states, locates or denies word stress; I re-opened all three held texts at the cited loci and confirmed every quoted sentence verbatim with correct page numbers, and a full-text search for stress/accent confirm 'stress' appears only in the 2011 abstract disclaimer and a Takale clitic gloss in 2017. These are the best and only phonological sources for this languoid per Glottolog and a Crossref search; the remaining unheld items (Moore 2019 MA morphology thesis; Wilde 2017 LTBA historical paper) are unlikely to contain a stress rule. Nothing was downloaded beyond bibliographic records (saved with; Coding and strength of the evidence stand; no action.

sources.citation: Watters, David E. (1973). Clause patterns in Kham. In Clause, sentence, and discourse patterns in selected languages of Nepal. Volume 1: General approach. Summer Institute of Linguistics. pp. 39-202.
sources.note: Describes Kham of the Taka-Sera (Takale) area, Baglung District — i.e. Takāle / Western Parbate Kham, not Gamāle Khām of Rolpā. It is also silent on stress, so it neither agrees with nor contradicts the (empty) catalog record.

sources.citation: Wilde, Christopher P. (2011). Observations on the phonology of Gamāle Khām. Himalayan Linguistics Journal 10. pp. 273-290.
sources.note: The catalog record for Gamāle Khām has an empty rule; Wilde 2011 gives no placement either, only the statement that stress patterns are yet to be determined and that a phonation/pitch (possibly tonal) contrast exists on words. The only 'stress' passage beyond the abstract is fn. 13 (p. 288) quoting Watters 2002: 38 on Takāle Khām tones T-1/T-2 being associated with 'intensity or stress' vs 'a lack of laryngeal stress' — that is about Takāle, not Gamāle, and about laryngeal register, not word-stress placement.
